questions.question: Q: Why does Odysseus disguise himself as a beggar rather than returning openly?
questions.correctAnswer: To assess who remains loyal, understand the suitors' strength, and plan his revenge without being targeted. Athena advises this strategy — it uses cunning rather than direct confrontation.

questions.question: Q: What is the significance of the bow contest?
questions.correctAnswer: Only Odysseus can string his own bow, proving his physical identity. The suitors cannot even bend it, showing their inferiority. Shooting through the twelve axes demonstrates unique skill that marks him as the true king.

questions.question: Q: How does Penelope test Odysseus's identity?
questions.correctAnswer: She mentions moving their marriage bed — but Odysseus knows it was built around a living olive tree and cannot be moved. This secret proves his identity more than any physical feat.

questions.question: Q: Is Odysseus's killing of the suitors justified?
questions.correctAnswer: In the moral world of the Odyssey, yes — they violated xenia, consumed his wealth, threatened his family and plotted to kill his son. Their punishment fits their crime and is sanctioned by the gods.

questions.question: Q: Why is the ending of the Odyssey ambiguous?
questions.correctAnswer: Athena intervenes to stop further bloodshed, but the families of the dead suitors want revenge. The poem ends with a fragile peace, suggesting that homecoming does not automatically resolve all conflicts.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response How far does the homecoming of Odysseus show that cunning is more important than strength? (15 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: Odysseus's homecoming demonstrates that cunning is essential, but it also shows that physical strength remains crucial — both are necessary for a complete hero. The entire strategy of the homecoming is built on cunning: Odysseus arrives in disguise, gathers intelligence from Eumaeus, tests the suitors' character as a beggar, and coordinates the ambush with Telemachus in secret. Without this clever planning, the suitors' superior numbers would have overwhelmed him. Penelope's own cunning — the shroud trick and the bow contest — creates the perfect opportunity for Odysseus to strike. The bed test is the ultimate proof of identity through knowledge, not strength. However, physical strength is also indispensable. Only Odysseus can string the great bow, a feat of pure physical power that no suitor can match. The actual battle in the great hall requires fighting skill and endurance — Odysseus, Telemachus and the two loyal servants must kill over a hundred suitors. Athena's intervention provides crucial divine support, but the combat is real and physically demanding. The homecoming succeeds precisely because Odysseus combines both qualities: cunning creates the opportunity and physical strength exploits it. Without cunning, strength would be overwhelmed by numbers; without strength, cunning would produce no result.
